Keynes' views on economics were challenged by Friedrich von Hayek, who argued that "the problem was that under central planning, there was no economic calculation--no way to make a rational decision to put this resource here or buy that good there, because there was no price system to weigh the alternatives." Central planners could make technical decisions but not economic ones. Over the rest of the century, that criticism would prove to be extraordinarily prescient. "Socialism shocked our generation," Hayek later said. Yet, he added, it profoundly altered the outlook of idealists returning from the war. "I know, for I was one of them.... Socialism told us that we had been looking for improvement in the wrong direction"(Stanislaw and Yergin 1998).

It should be pointed out that this argument was originally made by Ludwig von Mises. Indeed, Hayek's quoted statements above refer, not to socialism itself, but to Mises' book, "Socialism: An Economic and Sociological Analysis". Hayek wrote the foreword to the 1981 English edition:

When Socialism first appeared in 1922, its impact was profound. It gradually but fundamentally altered the outlook of many of the young idealists returning to their university studies after World War I. I know, for I was one of them.

We felt that the civilization in which we had grown up had collapsed. We were determined to build a better world, and it was this desire to reconstruct society that led many of us to the study of economics. Socialism promised to fulfill our hopes for a more rational, more just world. And then came this book. Our hopes were dashed. Socialism told us that we had been looking for improvement in the wrong direction.

I used to work in a slaughter house. The way we would drive cattle was get them really fat for a few weeks or months on sugar mixed with parts of other cattle that couldn't be sold, like bones and fat drippings. Then one day, we'd drive them single file into fenced paths. There would be lots of switch backs, over crowding, and random direction changes. Eventually, the lead cow would be separated from the rest walk up a ramp and the knocker would be waiting with an air compressed spike, called a knocker (both the person doing the killing and the tool he used were called knockers). He'd rest it on their brain stem and bam! The cow would go stiff, its eyes would roll back in its head, and the animal would start shaking. The goal was to minimize the amount of stress the animals go through because the stress causes them to make Cortisol, which damages the flavor of the meat.

Immediately after being knocked, a couple of guys would chain its hind legs to a conveyor belt and be taken further into the plant where a team would cut the hide off and pull the guts out. It was all very quick and we would average 1500 to 2000 animals a day. I was one of two gringos in the plant, couldn't speak Spanish, and was therefore useless. As a result, they gave me a shovel and put me under the conveyor belt to pick up any parts that fell off and put it into a garbage can to be mixed with the animal feed. I was lucky because they let me wear a rain coat, which was nice because the entire place was kept at just above freezing.

OP, when you describe driving humans like cattle, I can only hope you are wrong, but fear your analogy might almost be right...
Just the man I was looking for. What percentage of cows suffered in your experience? How many had to be re-stunned, or worse were processed without being re-stunned?

What percentage of cows suffered

It depends on how you define suffered. The factory did everything possible to keep the animals from stressing. Stress causes the animals to produce the hormones Adrenaline and Cortisol, which makes the meat taste bad, results in a lower quality final product, and a lower return on investment for the rancher. However, even as that is true, the animals were kept in over crowded concrete bottomed holding pens while they fattened up to slaughter weight. Cows want to be in green pastures. Corn silage is not a natural food for ruminants like cows. It's too woody. They don't digest it very well and much prefer field grass. However corn silage is cheap and the high sugar content improves the flavor of the meat.

How many had to be re-stunned, or worse were processed without being re-stunned?

They're not stunned. The knocker dissociates the brain stem from the rest of the body. In other words, their hearts are incapable of receiving signals to beat. I wasn't a knocker, so I don't know their error rate of missed attempts. I do not believe it was very high, because they got a lot of practice and its hard to screw up. However, they kept a 30-30 rifle by their side if anything went wrong. There was only one time while I was there that an animal got away. It was a big steer that got past the knocker area and ran through the production area. It ran past all the factory's bio-protection baths (bleach baths we had to walk through to get in and out of the factory), and ended up trapped in our break room. The knocker had to follow him in there and put the poor thing down. However, 1 fail in hundreds of thousands of slaughters is actually pretty impressive.
